name: Make a how-to video
summary: Teach one thing you can already do in a two-minute video somebody else could follow. The writing comes first: every step is a command, in order, with a time word in front of it.
subject: English Language
makes: a two-minute how-to video that teaches one skill, and the script it was filmed from
topics: Sentence Types, Adverbials, Formal & Informal Language
materials: Phone or tablet that records video|Something steady to rest it on — a pile of books works|Everything the skill itself needs|Paper for the storyboard × 2 sheets|A quiet room with daylight
steps: Choose one skill you can do well and can show in under two minutes — a card trick, a paper plane, plaiting hair, a keepy-up drill.|Write the steps as commands, one per line: "Fold the paper in half." Every step starts with a verb.|Put a time word in front of each step — first, next, after that, once that is done, finally — and never use the same one twice in a row.|Draw a storyboard: one box per step, with a sketch of what the camera sees and the exact words you will say underneath.|Film a ten-second test and watch it back. Can you hear yourself? Are your hands, not your head, in the middle of the frame?|Film each step as its own short clip, so a mistake only costs one clip. Redo any you are not happy with.|Trim the clips and put them in order in the phone's own editor. Add a title card that says what the viewer will be able to do by the end.|Watch it as somebody who has never done the skill. Find the one step where they would get lost, and re-film or re-word that step.
safety: Film at home, or ask before filming anywhere else. Keep your face, school uniform, address and anything with your name on it out of shot. The video stays with you — your tutor sees it at your next session.
share: Send your tutor your script — every step written as a command, with its time word — and say which step was hardest to film and why. Show the video itself at your next session.

name: A car gallery with the facts behind it
summary: Collect ten cars around a theme, give each one a fact card, then let the numbers decide who wins: put them in order, chart them, and find the average.
subject: Maths
makes: a gallery of ten cars, each with a photo and a fact card, and a bar chart comparing them
topics: Bar Charts & Pictograms, Ordering Numbers & Decimals, Units & Measures, Averages & Range
materials: Photos of ten cars — your own, or cut from a car magazine|Card or a slide document for the fact cards × 10|Squared paper × 2 sheets|Ruler|Glue stick, if the gallery is on paper
steps: Pick a theme so the cars can be compared fairly — the fastest you can find, the smallest, the oldest still on the road, electric cars, or the ten parked on your street.|Collect ten photos. If you take them yourself, photograph parked cars only and crop out number plates and people.|For every car find the same five facts: make and model, year, top speed in mph, 0–60 time in seconds, and length in metres. If one fact is missing, write "not found" rather than guessing.|Make one fact card per car: the photo, the five facts, and one sentence you would say about it to a friend.|Put the ten cars in order of top speed, fastest first. Then put them in order of 0–60 time. Are the two orders the same? Write one sentence on why they might not be.|Draw a bar chart of top speed on squared paper. Choose a scale where the tallest bar nearly fills the page, and label both axes with units.|Work out the mean top speed and the range. Which car is closest to the mean?|Give the gallery a title and lay the cards out in an order you can explain — by speed, by year, or by size.
safety: Stand on the pavement, never in the road, and photograph parked cars only. Look facts up with an adult on a trusted site — the maker's own pages are best — and note where each fact came from.
share: Send your tutor your theme, the fastest and slowest car on your chart, the mean top speed and the range. Bring the gallery itself to your next session.

name: Design and test a board game
summary: Invent a board game where the maths decides where the good and bad squares go, write rules someone else can follow, and change them after watching people play.
subject: Maths
makes: a playable board game with a written rules sheet, tested by at least two other people
topics: Basic Probability, Listing Outcomes & Sample Space, Relative Frequency & Expectation
materials: A3 card for the board|Dice × 2|Counters or small toys for pieces × 4|Blank cards for chance cards × 20|Coloured pens|Scissors
steps: Decide what the game is about and how somebody wins — first to the end, most points, or last one standing.|Sketch the board in pencil. A winding path of 40 to 60 squares is a good size.|List every total two dice can make in a 6 by 6 grid. Which total comes up most often? Put your best — or your worst — square that many places from the start.|Add special squares — move forward, miss a turn, take a card — and write down why each one is where it is.|Make 20 chance cards. Decide how many help and how many hurt, and write the chance of drawing a helpful one as a fraction.|Write the rules as numbered sentences that work without you in the room. Then ink the board.|Play it three times with family or friends. Tally how many turns each game took and who won.|Change the one rule that made it too long, too short or unfair, and play once more to see if the change worked.
safety: Cut on a table with the blade moving away from your other hand.
share: Send your tutor your rules, your grid of dice totals, the fraction of helpful chance cards, and how many turns each test game took. Say which rule you changed and what happened.

name: A stop-motion LEGO film
summary: Tell a three-part story with bricks and a phone, one photo at a time — and use frames per second to plan how many photos the film needs before you take the first one.
subject: Maths
makes: a stop-motion film of at least 20 seconds, with a title frame and an ending
materials: LEGO bricks and minifigures|A baseplate to build the set on|Phone or tablet with a free stop-motion app|Something to hold the phone still — a stand, or tape it to a box|A desk lamp|Blu Tack
steps: Write the story in three sentences: a beginning, a problem, and how it ends.|Storyboard it as six shots, one sketch per shot.|Plan the photos. At 12 frames per second a 20-second film needs 20 times 12, which is 240 photos. Share them between your six shots — which shot needs the most?|Build the set on the baseplate and stick the pieces that must not move down with Blu Tack.|Fix the phone and the lamp in place and close the curtains. Daylight changes while you work and makes the film flicker.|Move a figure a few millimetres, take a photo, and repeat. Small moves look smooth; big ones look jumpy.|Play each shot back as soon as it is done. Too fast? Add frames, or lower the frame rate — work out what 8 frames per second does to the length of the film.|Add a title frame, an end frame, and sound if the app allows it.
safety: Small pieces: keep loose bricks and Blu Tack away from younger brothers and sisters.
share: Send your tutor your three-sentence story, how many photos you took, the frame rate you chose, and how long the film came out — with the working that connects the three. Show the film at your next session.

name: A family recipe book
summary: Collect five recipes from your family, write them so anyone could cook them, and scale every one up and down — the maths cooks do without noticing.
subject: Maths
makes: a book of five family recipes, each with its story, its amounts in grams and millilitres, and versions for more and fewer people
topics: Direct Proportion, Ratio Problems, Best Value & Unitary Method, Units & Measures
materials: A notebook, or a document on a computer|Kitchen scales|Measuring jug|Five recipes collected from family|A phone for photos of the dishes|A shopping receipt or a supermarket website, for prices
steps: Ask five relatives for a recipe they cook often, and one sentence about where it comes from. That sentence goes at the top of the page.|Write every recipe the same way: how many it serves, the ingredients with amounts, then a numbered method.|Turn every amount into grams or millilitres. Weigh "a cup" or "a handful" on the scales rather than guessing.|Scale each recipe. If it serves 4, work out the amounts for 6 and for 2 — find one portion first, then multiply.|Cook one of the recipes with an adult and photograph it.|Use a receipt or a supermarket website to work out what one portion of that recipe costs.|Add a contents page and page numbers.|Read one method aloud to somebody who has never cooked it. Wherever they ask a question, the method needs another step.
safety: Cook only with an adult in the kitchen — hot pans, ovens and knives. Ask about allergies before anybody tastes anything.
share: Send your tutor one recipe scaled from 4 people to 6, with the working shown, and the cost of one portion. Bring the book to your next session.

name: Build a simple website about something you know
summary: Write three linked web pages by hand in HTML, about a subject you know better than most people your age, and make the writing fit a reader you have never met.
subject: English Language
makes: a three-page website, written in HTML, that opens in a browser and links between its pages
topics: Formal & Informal Language, Noun Phrases, Sentence Types
materials: A computer — typing code on a phone is miserable|A free code editor, or the computer's plain text editor|A web browser|A folder to keep the files in|Three or four photos you took yourself
steps: Choose a subject you know more about than most people your age — a game, a sport, an animal, a band, a place.|Plan three pages on paper: a home page, a page of facts, and a page of your own photos. Write each page's title and its first sentence.|Make a folder, and in it a file called index.html. Type the skeleton — html, head, title, body — and open the file in the browser.|Add a heading, two paragraphs and a list. Save and refresh after every change so you see each one work.|Make the other two pages and join all three with links, so you can click from any page to any other.|Add your photos, and give each one alt text that describes it for somebody who cannot see it.|Add a little style: a background colour, a font, and a maximum width so the lines are not too long to read.|Read every page aloud. Rewrite any sentence that sounds like you talking to a friend rather than to a visitor.
safety: The site stays on your computer and is not put online. Keep your full name, school, address and photos of people off it.
share: Send your tutor your three page titles and the first paragraph of your home page. Bring the folder on a memory stick, or open it on a laptop, at your next session.

name: A local history walk
summary: Find six things near home that are older than anyone you know, plan a walk between them with a map and a compass, and write the guide someone else could follow.
subject: Maths
makes: a walk of six stops near home, mapped to scale with bearings, and a one-sheet guide telling the story of each stop
topics: Scale Drawings & Maps, Bearings, Compound Measures
materials: A printed street map with a scale on it|A compass, or a compass app|A clipboard and pencil|A phone for photos and notes|Comfortable shoes
steps: With an adult, find six places within a short walk that are older than you: a war memorial, a plaque on a wall, a church, an old shop front, a date carved on a building, a post box with a king's or queen's initials.|Find out about each one — the date carved on it, the local library, or a local history society's website. Note where every fact came from.|Mark the six stops on the map and number them in walking order.|Measure each leg on the map and use the scale to work out the real distance. Add them up for the whole walk.|At each stop, take a bearing to the next one.|Walk it. Time each leg, and work out your average walking speed from the distance and the time.|Write a short paragraph for each stop: what it is, how old it is, and one thing a visitor would not notice unless somebody told them.|Put the map and the six paragraphs on one double-sided sheet that somebody else could follow without you.
safety: Always with an adult. Stay on pavements and paths, cross at crossings, and do not go onto private land.
share: Send your tutor the total distance worked out from the map, the time the walk took, your average speed, and the oldest date you found. Bring the guide sheet to your next session.

name: Record a podcast episode
summary: Plan, record and edit a ten-minute episode with an interview in it — where the hard part is the questions, and the second hardest is cutting what does not need to be there.
subject: English Language
makes: a ten-minute podcast episode with an introduction, a segment of your own, an interview and a sign-off
topics: Formal & Informal Language, Sentence Types, Standard English
materials: A phone with a voice recorder|A free audio editor|Headphones|A quiet room with soft furnishings — a wardrobe full of clothes makes a good studio|Somebody to interview
steps: Choose a topic and a listener: who is this for, and what should they know by the end?|Plan the running order: introduction (30 seconds), your own segment (3 minutes), the interview (5 minutes), round-up and sign-off (1 minute).|Write the introduction word for word. Write everything after it as bullet points — a script read out sounds stiff.|Write six interview questions. At least four must be open, so they cannot be answered with yes or no.|Record a 20-second test and listen on headphones for echo, hum and the fridge.|Record each part separately, so a mistake only costs that part.|In the editor, cut long pauses and false starts, then join the parts in order.|Listen to the whole episode once without stopping, and write down the time of anything you would change.
safety: Ask the person you interview before you record, and tell them who will hear it. Leave out surnames, schools and where anybody lives. The episode is not put online.
share: Send your tutor your topic, your six interview questions, and the time in the episode of the moment you are proudest of. Play it at your next session.
